Monday night: Tarun found his maths worksheet still blank at the bottom of his bag. He lay awake. Sir will shout. Sir will hit my hand with the ruler. Then the principal. Then a new school where nobody knows me, and Anand will sit with someone else forever. His stomach hurt.
Tuesday: In class he held out the blank sheet with shaking hands. Mr Dsouza glanced at it and said, 'Finish it tonight, Tarun. Bring it tomorrow.' That was all. Anand whispered, 'Told you. He said the same to me last week.'
Thursday: Tarun forgot his drawing book. His chest went tight, and then he remembered Tuesday. He wrote in his school diary: tell Sir, bring it tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Mr Dsouza say when he saw the blank worksheet?
qa.a: He said, 'Finish it tonight, Tarun. Bring it tomorrow.'

qa.q: Why did each step of Tarun's Monday-night story feel real to him?
qa.a: Tarun was scared and alone in the dark, so the ruler, the principal and the new school felt as if they had already happened 😰. His hurting stomach made the fear seem like proof.

qa.q: What turning point helped Tarun on Thursday?
qa.a: When he forgot the drawing book, Tarun remembered how small Tuesday really was and made a plan instead of a disaster: tell Sir and bring it the next day.

qa.q: How might Anand see Tarun's Monday-night worry?
qa.a: Anand had already forgotten homework and seen that Mr Dsouza only asks for it the next day, so to Anand the worry looks much bigger than the event, which is why Anand whispers 'Told you.'

grounding: Shows a child who forgot a worksheet leaping from a blank page to punishment, a new school and losing a friend, and the small real result on the next days.

passage: Shreya, come, sit. Worried about your notebook? Let me tell you about your Ammamma when she was ten. One morning I forgot my Kannada copy at home, and by the time the bus reached the school gate I had the whole thing planned. The teacher would twist my ear in front of everyone. Then the headmaster. Then my name would be struck off, and Appa would have to walk me home past the whole street, and everyone at the temple would know. I cried so hard in the corridor that the peon brought me water. And do you know what happened? Kamala Teacher said, 'Bring it tomorrow, Manjula.' Nothing else. I still remember how silly and how real it felt, both at once.

qa.q: What did young Manjula forget at home?
qa.a: Manjula forgot the Kannada copy at home.

qa.q: Why did Manjula cry in the corridor before the teacher had said anything?
qa.a: In Manjula's mind the ear-twisting, the headmaster, being struck off and the walk past the whole street had already happened, so the shame felt real before any of it came true.

qa.q: Why might Manjula's choice to tell this story help Shreya today?
qa.a: Hearing that the real ending was just 'Bring it tomorrow' gives Shreya a way to check a scary chain of thoughts against what usually happens.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel hearing that Ammamma once cried over a forgotten copy?
qa.a: Shreya may feel less alone and less silly 🙂, because a trusted grandparent had the same runaway worry and came through it fine.

grounding: Shows a grandmother recalling how, at ten, a forgotten copybook became imagined punishment, expulsion and public shame, when the real result was small.

Ma was at the hospital on her shift; nobody could bring it. His hands went cold. Late and no homework. Ma'am will make me stand outside. She'll write in my diary. The principal will see the diary. Mohit frowned. 'Last month I forgot mine twice. I just got a red line.' The van honked. Divyansh held on to that red line all the way to school.

qa.a: He could ask what really happened to others, like Mohit's red line, and plan one small step, such as telling Ma'am honestly at the start of class.

passage:
On the school bus in Delhi, Lokesh unzipped his bag and saw it: no EVS project file. It was still on the dining table, next to the fruit bowl.

His fingers went cold. Ma'am will be so angry. She'll send me to the principal. The principal will cane me, like in Dadaji's old stories. Then they'll throw me out. Everyone will know, forever.

Baljeet, beside him, looked up. "What happened?"

"I forgot my project file," Lokesh whispered. "I'm finished."

In class, he went to Ma'am's desk first, voice shaking. Ma'am looked up from the register. "Bring it tomorrow, Lokesh. Write it in your diary."

That was all. He walked back feeling light and a bit silly.

qa.q: Where had Lokesh left his EVS project file?
qa.a: It was still on the dining table, next to the fruit bowl.

qa.q: Why did "I'm finished" feel true to Lokesh on the bus?
qa.a: In his head, each step followed the last so quickly, from Ma'am's anger to the principal to a new school, that the worst ending felt certain. The cold fingers show how real the fear was.

qa.q: What small step helped Lokesh, and what could he try the next time his mind races?
qa.a: Going to Ma'am's desk first and telling her let him find out what really happens. Next time he could ask himself, "What usually happens when someone forgets?" before believing the worst.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Lokesh's reaction to one forgotten file?
qa.a: Baljeet might find it strange or even a bit funny that a forgotten file means being "finished". Baljeet could help by reminding Lokesh what happened last time someone forgot.

grounding: A boy who forgot his project file imagines being sent to the principal, caned, expelled and known forever, when the teacher only asks him to bring it tomorrow.

passage:
Anirban sat up in bed at ten o'clock. "Dada! Dada, wake up!"

Jeevan pulled the pillow off his face. "What happened?"

"The Bengali composition. I didn't write it. It's due tomorrow."

"Okay..."

"Not okay! Dipa Miss will shout. She'll make me stand on the bench. Then she'll hit my hand with the scale. Then she'll tell the headmistress, and they'll write a red letter to Baba, and I'll get thrown out. And everyone in the para will know!"

Jeevan sat up. "Wait, bhai. When Sourav forgot his last week, what happened?"

Anirban thought. "...She said bring it on Monday."

"Did anyone get thrown out?"

"No." A pause. "But she might this time."

"Write six lines before the bus. I'll wake you at six."

Anirban lay back down, but his eyes stayed open.

qa.q: What happened when Sourav forgot his composition last week?
qa.a: She said bring it on Monday.

qa.q: Why does Anirban still say "But she might this time" after remembering Sourav?
qa.a: The worry has already built a whole story, so one good example isn't enough to switch it off. His open eyes show the fear still feels real even though the facts point the other way.

qa.q: What worked in Jeevan's reply, and what could Jeevan add?
qa.a: Asking what really happened to Sourav brought Anirban back to facts, and offering to wake him at six gave a plan. Jeevan could also help him say the worst story aloud and check each step.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel being woken at ten over a composition?
qa.a: Jeevan might be sleepy and a little annoyed at first, but also see how scared Anirban is. Jeevan's calm questions suggest patience rather than irritation.

grounding: A boy who forgot his composition jumps from being scolded to being hit, reported and expelled, while his older brother gently checks the facts.
